title: Zhang Zhang to lead Monaco charity concert for Nepal relief - Monaco Life
description: Zhang Zhang to lead Monaco charity concert for Nepal relief  Monaco Life
publisher.title: Monaco Life
full_article:
Monaco-based violinist Zhang Zhang, a former member of the Monte-Carlo Philharmonic Orchestra, will take the stage at Stars of Monaco this Friday for a charity concert in aid of the victims of Nepal’s catastrophic floods, with all of the money raised going directly to relief efforts on the ground. The evening, on 18th September at 7pm, is the latest humanitarian appeal from Zhangmusiq, the Monaco NGO Zhang founded to turn live music into practical support.

The concert answers a tragedy that has shaken even seasoned observers. On 26th August, part of a glacier collapsed high in the Himalayas near the Nepal-China border, triggering a landslide and a wall of water and debris that tore down the Trishuli River valley. More than 1,300 people have been confirmed dead and thousands remain missing, making it Nepal’s deadliest natural disaster since the 2015 earthquake; scientists have linked the glacier’s collapse to a warming climate.

For Zhang, the footage was almost too much to take in. “Today, we are used to seeing so many AI-generated clips that, at first, I thought the footage was fake,” she told Monaco Life . “But I quickly realised that it was real.”

The decision to act, she said, came almost immediately. Born out of the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami and formally established in 2007, ZhangMusiq has built its work around moments like this. “Zhangomusiq was created in response to the Indian Ocean tsunami in 2004, so disaster relief is in our DNA,” she said.

Where the money goes

Every euro raised on the night will be sent to Nepal, in keeping with the NGO’s founding principle that 100% of funds reach the ground. The proceeds will be entrusted to the Himalayan Buddhist master His Eminence Kyabje Shyalpa Tenzin Rinpoche and his Nepal-based Universal Peace Sanctuary, to fund emergency medical care, shelter and food for survivors at their most vulnerable.

Zhang is keen that no contribution be seen as too small. “Sometimes the price of a nice cup of coffee or tea for us in Monaco can make a huge difference for someone somewhere in the world,” she said. It is a conviction rooted in her own childhood: born during China’s Cultural Revolution, she grew up sharing a nine-square-metre room with her family. “No help is too small,” she said.

Music as ‘the glue that keeps us connected’

On stage, Zhang will be joined by the jazz guitarist Leopoldo Giannola, her musical partner of some 25 years, for a programme that ranges freely from Bach to Bob Marley, taking in opera, film scores, French chansons, Chinese folk songs, tango and flamenco before the customary festive finale, when audiences are encouraged to sing and dance.

“Music is one of the few truly universal human expressions,” she said, describing it as “the glue that keeps us connected” in times of confusion and division — a way both to raise concrete support and to offer a shared moment of joy.

Beyond the immediate appeal, she hopes the evening also prompts reflection in Monaco on the mounting risks facing Himalayan communities as glaciers grow unstable. “We live in one of the most beautiful and safe places on the planet,” she said, “but climate change and environmental degradation affects all of us.”

How to attend or give

The concert takes place at Stars of Monaco, the reborn waterfront venue on Quai Antoine 1er, as part of the ‘Emergency Rescue Support for Nepal’ initiative. Those who cannot attend can donate directly through a QR code linked to the appeal.

“Come join us on Friday at Stars,” said Zhang. “Let’s create some joy together, while offering friendship and love to the people of Nepal.”

title: Why has the response to Nepal’s floods been so muted? - Al Jazeera
description: Why has the response to Nepal’s floods been so muted?  Al Jazeera
publisher.title: Al Jazeera
full_article:
It has been three weeks since the collapse of a glacier and rock mass from the Langtang Lirung mountain triggered devastating floods in Nepal’s Bhotekoshi and Trishuli valleys. Officials have confirmed the loss of more than 1,380 precious lives, while around 5,100 remain missing. The disaster shattered thousands of homes and wiped out vital infrastructure.

Nepal government’s rapid assessment estimates that full recovery and long-term reconstruction will need $4.7bn. That is roughly 10 percent of Nepal’s annual gross domestic product (GDP), and more than a third of its federal budget.

And yet, despite considerable media and public attention, the international political response has remained strikingly muted.

We have heard some condolence messages from foreign governments, along with emergency supplies and pledges of help. These matter. But the response mainly targeted immediate humanitarian aid. For instance, the United States pledged $3.6m, the United Kingdom $6m, and the European Union $2.3m. But these meagre funds cannot meet the needs of affected communities and provide them with the shelter, food and infrastructure to survive the winter.

Why has the response been so inadequate? Why have so few political leaders spoken up about this disaster with the urgency its scale demands?

Part of the answer may lie in an uncomfortable question Nepal has now put directly on the table: who should pay for climate loss and damage?

Nepal is increasingly framing the floods not simply as another weather-induced catastrophe, but as a consequence of a climate crisis to which the country contributed almost nothing.

Advertisement

This points to a deeper inequality of climate crisis.

For over a century, wealthy countries have consumed a vastly disproportionate share of the atmosphere’s capacity to absorb carbon dioxide. They grew their economies through industrialisation driven by fossil fuel consumption. Meanwhile, countries like Nepal got little chance to use anything approaching an equivalent share of that atmospheric space.

The result shows a stark divide between those who benefitted disproportionately from burning fossil fuels and those who face growing consequences.

Nepal has argued that international support to deal with climate catastrophe is not a charity. It must be climate justice. It has asked the United Nations’ Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage for urgent support, and the fund’s board is now considering how to respond.

That changes the political conversation. And it takes us back to the bargain struck in Paris a decade ago.

Developing countries fought hard for the international climate regime under the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change to recognise “loss and damage” or the destruction that cannot simply be prevented through mitigation or adapted to. They secured its recognition in Article 8 of the Paris Agreement.

But wealthy countries drew a line around what that recognition could mean. The decision text adopted alongside the Paris Agreement states that Article 8 “does not involve or provide a basis for any liability or compensation”.

It was a strange political bargain: the world could acknowledge climate-related loss and damage, but that acknowledgement could not lead to demands for compensation.

Nepal is now testing the limits of that bargain.

The legal picture is more complicated than simply saying that the Paris Agreement prohibits climate compensation. In 2025, the International Court of Justice ruled that countries have a legal obligation to protect the climate system; if they fail their obligations, they are liable for reparations or compensation for the damage they have caused. The decision sparked renewed attention to the questions around state responsibility under international law.

In the case of Nepal and other developing countries disproportionately affected by the climate crisis, the state does not need to prove that one particular country caused a specific flood before the international community can recognise a responsibility to address the consequences of climate change.

But there is another issue: the traditional international system for supporting developing countries is itself shrinking. At precisely the time climate losses are mounting, official development assistance is falling. It plummeted by 23.1 percent in 2025, the largest annual contraction on record. Humanitarian assistance also fell sharply.

Advertisement

And the problem is not simply that there is too little aid.

For decades, the global economy has transferred enormous amounts of wealth and resources through unequal economic ties between the Global North and the Global South. Climate finance won’t fix that imbalance if it simply returns a fraction of that wealth as loans or private investment options.

A country should not have to borrow its way out of a climate disaster it did little to create.

Nor can compensation substitute for mitigation. Wealthy countries cannot keep consuming a disproportionate share of the world’s energy and material resources while ignoring the consequences elsewhere. They must rapidly reduce their own emissions and ecological overconsumption.

The muted response to the floods in Nepal therefore raises a larger question about international cooperation.

Perhaps the world is comfortable acknowledging the growing cost of the climate crisis. It is much less comfortable when countries affected ask whether the costs should be borne by those who contributed most to creating the crisis.

The avenues for changing this already exist: the Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage, the UN climate negotiations, and the evolving body of international law on climate responsibility.

What is missing is the political recognition that the costs of climate destruction cannot indefinitely be treated as somebody else’s problem.

If climate justice means anything, it must eventually include reparations for the damage caused by an unequal appropriation of the atmospheric commons.

That conversation can no longer be postponed.

title: Reaching Families Cut Off by Floodwaters in Nepal - All Hands & Hearts
description: Reaching Families Cut Off by Floodwaters in Nepal  All Hands & Hearts
publisher.title: All Hands & Hearts
full_article:
Three weeks after the floods, many of Nepal’s hardest-hit communities are still cut off from road access. Almost 1,400 people have been confirmed dead, and more than 5,000 are still reported missing. Bridges that once connected a single, intact community are gone, and the river now divides daily life, forcing people to cross in makeshift cable car systems.

Our teams are on the ground supporting displaced families, providing supplies for the respectful care of the deceased, and distributing generators and power equipment. We’re also helping communities clean and disinfect homes and schools to prevent disease, mold, and contamination, and building shower facilities so families can hold onto some sense of dignity and stability in the middle of all this.

AH&H-made shower blocks for communities to use in Nuwakot AH&H volunteers build a secure fence around a school in Tupche, Nuwakot

Schools have become a particular focus. We’re providing students with learning kits, early childhood development learning toys, educational games, slippers, and other essentials to help them get back to some version of normal. A secondary school that had been serving as a relocation center for displaced families needed help returning to its original purpose, so our team deep-cleaned and disinfected nine classrooms, moved desks, and scrubbed floors so the school can reopen as soon as possible. In Nuwakot, we’re also building a secure fence around a school along the riverbank to keep students safe and away from unstable ground near the water. It’s a small change with a real impact: a safer space to learn, and one less thing for children already carrying so much to worry about. By supporting both students and teachers, we’re helping create the continuity that lets kids keep learning, playing, and moving forward, even in the hardest circumstances.

Distribution of educational support materials to continue kids education Disinfection of classrooms being used as a holding center for affected families

As communities move from emergency response toward recovery, we will continue addressing their most urgent needs and helping them rebuild safely. Over the next two years, we aim to raise $5 million to rebuild 20 schools in communities that need them most, building on our years of work in Nepal and helping create safer, stronger places for children and families to rebuild their lives.

title: Nepal raises the number of people missing in the deadly mudslide to 6,150 - voz.us

Published by AFP 16 de septiembre, 2026

Topics: Nepal

Top stories

The disaster management authority of Nepal reported Wednesday that the number of missing people had risen to 6,150, a significant upward revision of the death toll from the Aug. 26 mudslide.

The new tally added nearly 1,000 missing persons to the figure of 5,179 reported on Tuesday.

"We have been compiling information on the missing from district offices and have revised the data following verification," disaster agency spokeswoman Shanti Mahat told AFP.

The number of bodies recovered stands at 1,403, of which 105 have been identified, according to the disaster agency.

Across the border, in China, the toll stands at 43 dead and 519 missing, according to state media.

The death toll in both countries following the glacier collapse on the mountain on the Nepal-China border now stands at 1,446 dead and at least 6,669 missing.

Among the missing are several hundred foreigners, including tourists and pilgrims.

“We have been collecting details on the missing people from the district offices and revised the data after verification,” disaster authority spokesperson Shanti Mahat told AFP.

The figure rose from the 5,179 reported a day earlier.

The number of bodies recovered stood at 1,403, of which 105 had been identified, according to the disaster agency.

Across the border in China, 43 people were dead and 519 were missing, according to state media.

The combined toll from the deadly glacial mountain collapse on the Nepal-China border stood at 1,446 people dead and at least 6,669 missing in the two countries.

Several hundred foreigners, including tourists and pilgrims, were among those missing.

The scale of the flood was unlike anything witnesses had seen before, with the Nepali government pointing to the severe effects of rising global temperatures on the Himalayan mountains.

Nepal, a largely rural nation of 30 million people, contributes a fraction of the global greenhouse gas emissions produced by industrialized nations.

Prime Minister Balendra Shah will make his first foreign trip as leader to address the U.N. General Assembly on the urgent issue next week.
